title: Coverage routes can expand while a large uninsured gap remains
source_unit: CDC National Center for Health Statistics preliminary 2025 National Health Interview Survey health insurance estimates
geography: United States civilian noninstitutionalized population; 2021-2025 survey estimates

denominator.unit: U.S. civilian noninstitutionalized population interviewed in NHIS

older_adults.unit: adults age 65 and older uninsured at interview

observations.method: Preliminary NHIS household interview estimates; insurance categories follow CDC definitions and are weighted survey estimates.
observations.uncertainty: Early-release estimates are based on preliminary data before final editing and weighting; CDC says differences from final products are typically less than or equal to 0.5 percentage points.
observations.subgroup: All ages, children, working-age adults, and older adults in the civilian noninstitutionalized population.
observations.counterinterpretation: A stable uninsured rate can coexist with meaningful changes in coverage type, continuity, or affordability that this release does not measure.

observations.period: 2021-2025; exchange coverage and selected subgroup patterns

denominator.unit: people younger than age 65 in NHIS

exchange_coverage.value: 6.3% or 17.4 million in 2025, up from 4.3% or 11.6 million in 2021

observations.method: NHIS descriptive estimates by coverage type, age, and race or ethnicity; comparisons include reported statistical significance.
observations.uncertainty: The survey does not identify which policy or enrollment event caused the changes and does not measure whether coverage was affordable or used.
observations.subgroup: People younger than 65, adults ages 18-64, and Hispanic adults ages 18-64.
observations.counterinterpretation: Exchange growth and lower subgroup uninsurance can represent real access gains even while the national uninsured rate remains stable.

boundary: This record measures preliminary insurance status and coverage-type trends from NHIS. It does not establish continuity, affordability, network access, care use, medical debt, health outcomes, or causal policy effects.
